{{Short description|Series related to Ramanujan's pi formulas}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Ramanujan–Sato series'''<ref name = "Chan 1">{{cite journal |first1=Heng Huat |last1=Chan |first2=Song Heng |last2=Chan |first3=Zhiguo |last3=Liu |title=Domb's numbers and Ramanujan–Sato type series for 1/{{pi}} |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |volume=186 |issue=2 |year=2004 |pages=396–410 |doi=10.1016/j.aim.2003.07.012 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name = "Almkvist">{{cite book |first1=Gert |last1=Almkvist |first2=Jesus |last2=Guillera |year=2013 |chapter=Ramanujan–Sato-Like Series |editor-last=Borwein |editor-first=J. |editor2-last=Shparlinski |editor2-first=I. |editor3-last=Zudilin |editor3-first=W. |title=Number Theory and Related Fields |series=Springer Proceedings in Mathematics & Statistics |volume=43 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-6641-3 |pages=55–74 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-6642-0_2 |s2cid=44875082 }}</ref> generalizes [[Srinivasa Ramanujan|Ramanujan]]'s [[List of formulae involving π#Infinite series|pi formulas]] such as,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{2 \sqrt 2}{99^2} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(4k)!}{k!^4} \frac{26390k+1103}{396^{4k}}</math>

to the form

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty s(k) \frac{Ak+B}{C^k}</math>

by using other well-defined [[sequence]]s of [[integer]]s <math>s(k)</math> obeying a certain [[recurrence relation]], sequences which may be expressed in terms of [[binomial coefficient]]s <math>\tbinom{n}{k}</math>, and <math>A,B,C</math> employing [[modular form]]s of higher levels.

Ramanujan made the enigmatic remark that there were "corresponding theories", but it was only in 2012 that H. H. Chan and S. Cooper found a general approach that used the underlying modular [[congruence subgroup]] <math>\Gamma_0(n)</math>,<ref name="Chan 3">{{cite journal |first1=Heng Huat |last1=Chan |first2=Shaun |last2=Cooper |title=Rational analogues of Ramanujan's series for <var>1/π</var> |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=153 |issue=2 |year=2012 |pages=361–383 |doi=10.1017/S0305004112000254 |s2cid=76656590 |url=http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/6810/c8ac1ad01821a504e66f5d8665aeeae93cab.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219004315/http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/6810/c8ac1ad01821a504e66f5d8665aeeae93cab.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2019-12-19 }}</ref> while G. Almkvist has [[experimental mathematics|experimentally]] found numerous other examples also with a general method using [[differential operators]].<ref>{{cite arXiv |first=G. |last=Almkvist |title=Some conjectured formulas for <var>1/π</var> coming from polytopes, K3-surfaces and Moonshine |date=2012 |class=math.NT |eprint=1211.6563 }}</ref>

Levels '''''1–4A''''' were given by Ramanujan (1914),<ref>{{cite journal |first=S. |last=Ramanujan |title=Modular equations and approximations to <var>π</var> |journal=Quart. J. Math. |location=Oxford |volume=45 |year=1914 |pages=350–372|url=http://ramanujan.sirinudi.org/Volumes/published/ram06.html}}</ref> level '''''5''''' by H. H. Chan and S. Cooper (2012),<ref name="Chan 3"/>  '''''6A''''' by Chan, Tanigawa, Yang, and Zudilin,<ref name = "CTYZ">{{cite journal |last1=Chan |last2=Tanigawa |last3=Yang |last4=Zudilin |title=New analogues of Clausen's identities arising from the theory of modular forms |year=2011 |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |volume=228 |issue=2 |pages=1294–1314 |doi=10.1016/j.aim.2011.06.011 |doi-access=free |hdl=1959.13/934806 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>  '''''6B''''' by Sato (2002),<ref name = "Sato">{{cite journal |first=T. |last=Sato |title=Apéry numbers and Ramanujan's series for 1/{{pi}} |journal=Abstract of a Talk Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Mathematical Society of Japan |year=2002 }}</ref> '''''6C''''' by H. Chan, S. Chan, and Z. Liu (2004),<ref name="Chan 1"/> '''''6D''''' by H. Chan and H. Verrill (2009),<ref name = "Chan 2">{{cite journal |first1=H. |last1=Chan |first2=H. |last2=Verrill |title=The Apéry numbers, the Almkvist–Zudilin Numbers, and new series for 1/π |year=2009 |journal=Mathematical Research Letters |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=405–420 |doi=10.4310/MRL.2009.v16.n3.a3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> level '''''7''''' by S. Cooper (2012),<ref name = "Cooper 1">{{cite journal |first=S. |last=Cooper |title=Sporadic sequences, modular forms and new series for 1/π |journal=Ramanujan Journal |year=2012 |volume=29 |issue=1–3 |pages=163–183 |doi=10.1007/s11139-011-9357-3 |s2cid=122870693 }}</ref> part of level '''''8''''' by Almkvist and [[Jesús Guillera|Guillera]] (2012),<ref name="Almkvist"/>  part of level '''''10''''' by Y. Yang, and the rest by H. H. Chan and S. Cooper.

The notation ''j''<sub>''n''</sub>(''τ'') is derived from [[Don Zagier|Zagier]]<ref name = "Zagier">{{cite web |first=D. |last=Zagier |title=Traces of Singular Moduli |pages=15–16 |date=2000 |url=https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/tex/TracesSingModuli/fulltext.pdf }}</ref> and ''T''<sub>''n''</sub> refers to the relevant [http://oeis.org/wiki/Index_to_OEIS:_Section_Mat#McKay_Thompson McKay–Thompson series].

==Level 1==

Examples for levels 1–4 were given by Ramanujan in his 1917 paper. Given  <math>q=e^{2\pi i \tau}</math> as in the rest of this article. Let,

:<math>\begin{align}
j(\tau) &= \left(\frac{E_4(\tau)}{\eta^8(\tau)}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{q} + 744 + 196884q + 21493760q^2 +\cdots\\
j^*(\tau) &= 432\,\frac{\sqrt{j(\tau)}+ \sqrt{j(\tau)-1728}}{\sqrt{j(\tau)}- \sqrt{j(\tau)-1728}} = \frac{1}{q}  - 120 + 10260q - 901120q^2 + \cdots
\end{align}</math>

with the [[j-invariant|j-function]] ''j''(''τ''), [[Eisenstein series]] ''E''<sub>4</sub>, and [[Dedekind eta function]] ''η''(''τ''). The first expansion is the McKay–Thompson series of class 1A ({{OEIS2C|id= A007240}}) with a(0) = 744. Note that, as first noticed by [[John McKay (mathematician)|J. McKay]], the coefficient of the linear term of ''j''(''τ'') almost equals 196883, which is the degree of the smallest nontrivial [[irreducible representation]] of the [[monster group]], a relationship called [[monstrous moonshine]]. Similar phenomena will be observed in the other levels. Define

:<math>s_{1A}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\binom{3k}{k}\binom{6k}{3k}=1, 120, 83160, 81681600,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A001421}})

:<math>s_{1B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{2j}{j}\binom{3j}{j}\binom{6j}{3j}\binom{k+j}{k-j}(-432)^{k-j} =1, -312, 114264, -44196288,\ldots</math>

Then the two modular functions and sequences are related by

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{1A}(k)\,\frac{1}{(j(\tau))^{k+\frac12}}= \pm \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{1B}(k)\,\frac{1}{(j^*(\tau))^{k+\frac12}}</math>

if the series converges and the sign chosen appropriately, though squaring both sides easily removes the ambiguity. Analogous relationships exist for the higher levels.

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 12\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{1A}(k)\,\frac{163\cdot3344418k+13591409}{\left(-640320^3\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-163}}{2}\right)=-640320^3=-262537412640768000</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 24\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{1B}(k)\,\frac{-3669+320\sqrt{645}\,\left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left({-432}\,U_{645}^3\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j^*\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-43}}{2}\right) = -432\,U_{645}^{3}=-432\left(\frac{127+5\sqrt{645}}{2}\right)^{3}</math>

where <math>645=43\times15,</math> and <math>U_n</math> is a [[Fundamental unit (number theory)|fundamental unit]]. The first belongs to a [[Chudnovsky algorithm|family of formulas]] that were rigorously proven by the Chudnovsky brothers in 1989<ref>{{Citation|last1=Chudnovsky|first1=David V.|author1-link=Chudnovsky brothers|last2=Chudnovsky|first2=Gregory V.|author2-link=Chudnovsky brothers|title=The Computation of Classical Constants|year=1989|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|issn=0027-8424|volume=86|issue=21|pages=8178–8182|doi=10.1073/pnas.86.21.8178|pmid=16594075|pmc=298242|jstor=34831|bibcode=1989PNAS...86.8178C|doi-access=free}}.</ref> 
and later used to calculate 10 trillion digits of π in 2011.<ref>{{citation|title=10 Trillion Digits of Pi: A Case Study of summing Hypergeometric Series to high precision on Multicore Systems|last1=Yee|first1=Alexander|last2=Kondo|first2=Shigeru|series=Technical Report|year=2011|publisher=Computer Science Department, University of Illinois|hdl=2142/28348}}.</ref> The second formula, and the ones for higher levels, were established by H.H. Chan and S. Cooper in 2012.<ref name="Chan 3"/>

==Level 2==

Using Zagier's notation<ref name = "Zagier" /> for the modular function of level 2,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{2A}(\tau) &=\left(\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)}\right)^{12}+2^6 \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right)^{12}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{q} + 104 + 4372q + 96256q^2 + 1240002q^3+\cdots \\
j_{2B}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)}\right)^{24} = \frac{1}{q} - 24 + 276q - 2048q^2 + 11202q^3 - \cdots
\end{align}</math>

Note that the coefficient of the linear term of ''j''<sub>2A</sub>(''τ'') is one more than 4371 which is the smallest degree greater than 1 of the irreducible representations of the [[Baby Monster group#Generalized Monstrous Moonshine|Baby Monster group]]. Define,

:<math>s_{2A}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2k}{k}\binom{4k}{2k}=1, 24, 2520, 369600, 63063000,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A008977}})

:<math>s_{2B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{2j}{j}\binom{2j}{j}\binom{4j}{2j}\binom{k+j}{k-j}(-64)^{k-j}=1, -40, 2008, -109120, 6173656,\ldots</math>

Then,

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{2A}(k)\,\frac{1}{(j_{2A}(\tau))^{k+\frac12}}= \pm \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{2B}(k)\,\frac{1}{(j_{2B}(\tau))^{k+\frac12}}</math>

if the series converges and the sign chosen appropriately.

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 32\sqrt{2}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{2A}(k)\,\frac{58\cdot455k+1103}{\left(396^4\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{2A}\left(\frac\sqrt{-58}{2}\right)=396^4=24591257856</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 16\sqrt{2}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{2B}(k)\,\frac{-24184+9801\sqrt{29}\, \left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(64\,U_{29}^{12}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{2B}\left(\frac\sqrt{-58}{2}\right)=64\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{29}}{2}\right)^{12}=64\,U_{29}^{12}</math>

The first formula, found by Ramanujan and mentioned at the start of the article, belongs to a family proven by D. Bailey and the Borwein brothers in a 1989 paper.<ref>{{cite journal |authorlink=Jonathan Borwein |first1=J. M. |last1=Borwein |authorlink2=Peter Borwein |first2=P. B. |last2=Borwein |first3=D. H. |last3=Bailey |title=Ramanujan, modular equations, and approximations to pi; Or how to compute one billion digits of pi |journal=Amer. Math. Monthly |volume=96 |year=1989 |issue=3 |pages=201–219 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1989.11972169 |url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/pubs/amm_supplements/Monthly_Reference_1.pdf}}</ref>

==Level 3==

Define,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{3A}(\tau) &=\left(\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(3\tau)}\right)^{6}+3^3 \left(\frac{\eta(3\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right)^{6}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{q} + 42 + 783q + 8672q^2 +65367q^3+\cdots\\
j_{3B}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(3\tau)}\right)^{12} = \frac{1}{q} - 12 + 54q - 76q^2 - 243q^3 + 1188q^4 +  \cdots\\
\end{align}</math>

where 782 is the smallest degree greater than 1 of the irreducible representations of the [[Fischer group Fi23#Generalized Monstrous Moonshine|Fischer group]] ''Fi''<sub>23</sub> and,

:<math>s_{3A}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2k}{k}\binom{3k}{k}=1, 12, 540, 33600, 2425500,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A184423}})

:<math>s_{3B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{2j}{j}\binom{2j}{j}\binom{3j}{j}\binom{k+j}{k-j}(-27)^{k-j}=1, -15, 297, -6495, 149481,\ldots</math>

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 2\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{3A}(k)\,\frac{267\cdot53k+827}{\left(-300^3\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{3A}\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{-267}}{6}\right) = -300^3 = -27000000</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{3B}(k)\,\frac{12497-3000\sqrt{89}\, \left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(-27\,U_{89}^{2}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{3B}\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{-267}}{6}\right)=-27\,\left(500+53\sqrt{89}\right)^2=-27\,U_{89}^{2}</math>

==Level 4==

Define,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{4A}(\tau)&=\left(\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(4\tau)}\right)^{4}+4^2 \left(\frac{\eta(4\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right)^{4}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\eta^2(2\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(4\tau)} \right)^{24} =-\left(\frac{\eta\left(\frac{2\tau+3}{2}\right)}{\eta(2\tau+3)} \right)^{24} = \frac{1}{q} + 24+ 276q + 2048q^2 +11202q^3+\cdots\\
j_{4C}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(4\tau)}\right)^{8} = \frac{1}{q} -8 + 2
q - 62q^3 + 216q^5 - 641q^7 +  \ldots\\
\end{align}</math>

where the first is the 24th power of the [[Weber modular function]] <math>\mathfrak{f}(2\tau)</math>. And,

:<math>s_{4A}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}^3=1, 8, 216, 8000, 343000,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A002897}})

:<math>s_{4C}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{2j}{j}^3\binom{k+j}{k-j}(-16)^{k-j}= (-1)^k \sum_{j=0}^k\binom{2j}{j}^2\binom{2k-2j}{k-j}^2 =1, -8, 88, -1088, 14296,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A036917}})

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 8\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{4A}(k)\,\frac{6k+1}{\left(-2^9\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{4A}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-4}}{2}\right)=-2^9=-512</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 16\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{4C}(k)\,\frac{1-2\sqrt{2}\, \left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(-16\,U_{2}^{4}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{4C}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-4}}{2}\right) = -16\,\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)^4=-16\,U_{2}^{4}</math>

==Level 5==

Define,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{5A}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)}\right)^{6}+5^3 \left(\frac{\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right)^{6}+22 =\frac{1}{q} + 16 + 134q + 760q^2 +3345q^3+\cdots\\
j_{5B}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)}\right)^{6}= \frac{1}{q}- 6 + 9q + 10q^2 - 30q^3 + 6q^4 + \cdots
\end{align}</math>

and,

:<math>s_{5A}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2\binom{k+j}{j} =1, 6, 114, 2940, 87570,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{5B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{j+k}\binom{k}{j}^3\binom{4k-5j}{3k}=1, -5, 35, -275, 2275, -19255,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A229111}})

where the first is the product of the [[central binomial coefficient]]s and the Apéry numbers ({{OEIS2C|id=A005258}})<ref name="Cooper 1"/>

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{5}{9}\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{5A}(k)\,\frac{682k+71}{(-15228)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{5A}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{-5(47)}}{10}\right)=-15228=-(18\sqrt{47})^2</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{5B}(k)\,\frac{25\sqrt{5}-141\left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(-5\sqrt{5}\,U_{5}^{15}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{5B}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{-5(47)}}{10}\right)=-5\sqrt{5}\,\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{15}=-5\sqrt{5}\,U_{5}^{15}</math>

==Level 6==

===Modular functions===

In 2002, Takeshi Sato<ref name="Sato"/> established the first results for levels above 4. It involved [[Apéry's theorem|Apéry numbers]] which were first used to establish the irrationality of <math>\zeta(3)</math>. First, define,

:<math>\begin{align}j_{6A}(\tau) &=\left(\sqrt{j_{6B}(\tau)} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{j_{6B}(\tau)}}\right)^2 = \left(\sqrt{j_{6C}(\tau)} + \frac{8}{\sqrt{j_{6C}(\tau)}}\right)^2 = \left(\sqrt{j_{6D}(\tau)} + \frac{9}{\sqrt{j_{6D}(\tau)}}\right)^2-4 =\frac{1}{q} + 10 + 79q + 352q^2 +\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{6B}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta(3\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\eta(6\tau)}\right)^{12}=\frac{1}{q} + 12 + 78q + 364q^2 + 1365q^3+\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{6C}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(3\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\eta(6\tau)}\right)^{6}=\frac{1}{q} -6 + 15q -32q^2 + 87q^3-192q^4+\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{6D}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(3\tau)\eta(6\tau)}\right)^{4}=\frac{1}{q} -4 - 2q + 28q^2 - 27q^3 - 52q^4+\cdots\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{6E}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta^3(3\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\eta^3(6\tau)}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{q} +3 + 6q + 4q^2 - 3q^3 - 12q^4 +\cdots\end{align}</math>

The phenomenon of <math>j_{6A}</math> being squares or a near-square of the other functions will also be manifested by <math>j_{10A}</math>. Another similarity between levels 6 and 10 is J. Conway and S. Norton showed there are linear relations between the McKay–Thompson series ''T''<sub>''n''</sub>,<ref>{{cite journal |first1=J. |last1=Conway |first2=S. |last2=Norton |title=Monstrous Moonshine |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=11 |issue=3 |year=1979 |pages=308–339 [p. 319] |doi=10.1112/blms/11.3.308 }}</ref> one of which was,

:<math>T_{6A}-T_{6B}-T_{6C}-T_{6D}+2T_{6E} = 0</math>

or using the above eta quotients ''j''<sub>''n''</sub>,

:<math>j_{6A}-j_{6B}-j_{6C}-j_{6D}+2j_{6E} = 22</math>

A similar relation exists for level 10.

===α Sequences===

For the modular function '''''j''<sub>6A</sub>''', one can associate it with ''three'' different sequences. (A similar situation happens for the level 10 function '''''j''<sub>10A</sub>'''.) Let,

:<math>\alpha_1(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^3 =1, 4, 60, 1120, 24220,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A181418}}, labeled as ''s''<sub>6</sub> in Cooper's paper)

:<math>\alpha_2(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}\sum_{m=0}^j\binom{j}{m}^3=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2\binom{2j}{j} =1, 6, 90, 1860, 44730,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A002896}})

:<math>\alpha_3(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}(-8)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j\binom{j}{m}^3 =1, -12, 252, -6240, 167580, -4726512,\ldots</math>

The three sequences involve the product of the [[central binomial coefficient]]s <math>c(k)=\tbinom{2k}{k}</math> with: first, the [http://mathworld.wolfram.com/FranelNumber.html Franel numbers] <math>\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^k \tbinom{k}{j}^3</math>; second, {{OEIS2C|id=A002893}}, and third, <math>(-1)^k</math> {{OEIS2C|id=A093388}}. Note that the second sequence, ''α''<sub>2</sub>(''k'') is also the number of 2''n''-step polygons on a [[Integer lattice|cubic lattice]]. Their complements,

:<math>\alpha'_2(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}(-1)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j\binom{j}{m}^3 =1, 2, 42, 620, 12250,\ldots</math>

:<math>\alpha'_3(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}(8)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j\binom{j}{m}^3 =1, 20, 636, 23840, 991900,\ldots</math>

There are also associated sequences, namely the Apéry numbers,

:<math>s_{6B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2\binom{k+j}{j}^2 =1, 5, 73, 1445, 33001,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A005259}})

the Domb numbers (unsigned) or the number of 2''n''-step polygons on a [[Diamond cubic#Mathematical structure|diamond lattice]],

:<math>s_{6C}(k)=(-1)^k \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2 \binom{2(k-j)}{k-j} \binom{2j}{j} =1, -4, 28, -256, 2716,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A002895}})

and the Almkvist-Zudilin numbers,

:<math>s_{6D}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j}\,3^{k-3j}\,\frac{(3j)!}{j!^3} \binom{k}{3j} \binom{k+j}{j} =1, -3, 9, -3, -279, 2997,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A125143}})

where

:<math>\frac{(3j)!}{j!^3}=\binom{2j}{j}\binom{3j}{j}</math>

===Identities===

The modular functions can be related as,

:<math> P = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_1(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}} =  \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_2(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)+4\right)^{k+\frac12}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_3(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)-32\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

:<math> Q = \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6B}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6B}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}}= \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6C}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6C}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}}= \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6D}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6D}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

if the series converges and the sign chosen appropriately. It can also be observed that,

:<math>P = Q = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha'_2(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)-4\right)^{k+\frac12}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha'_3(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)+32\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

which implies,

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_2(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)+4\right)^{k+\frac12}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha'_2(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{6A}(\tau)-4\right)^{k+\frac12}} </math>

and similarly using α<sub>3</sub> and α'<sub>3</sub>.

===Examples===

One can use a value for '''''j''<sub>6A</sub>''' in three ways. For example, starting with,

:<math>\Delta=j_{6A}\left(\sqrt{\frac{-17}{6}}\right)=198^2-4=\left(140\sqrt{2}\right)^2=39200</math>

and noting that <math>3\cdot17=51</math> then,

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{24\sqrt{3}}{35}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_1(k)\,\frac{51\cdot11k+53}{(\Delta)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{99}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_2(k)\,\frac{17\cdot560k+899}{(\Delta+4)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha_3(k)\,\frac{770k+73}{(\Delta-32)^{k+\frac12}}\\ 
\end{align}</math>

as well as,

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{12\sqrt{3}}{9799}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha'_2(k)\,\frac{11\cdot51\cdot560k+29693}{(\Delta-4)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{6\sqrt{3}}{613}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \alpha'_3(k)\,\frac{51\cdot770k+3697}{(\Delta+32)^{k+\frac12}}\\ 
\end{align}</math>

though the formulas using the complements apparently do not yet have a rigorous proof. For the other modular functions,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 8\sqrt{15}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6B}(k)\,\left(\frac12-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{20}+k\right)\left(\frac{1}{\phi^{12}}\right)^{k+\frac12},
\quad j_{6B}\left(\sqrt{\frac{-5}{6}}\right)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{12}=\phi^{12}</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac12\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6C}(k)\,\frac{3k+1}{32^k},
\quad j_{6C}\left(\sqrt{\frac{-1}{3}}\right)=32</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 2\sqrt{3}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{6D}(k)\,\frac{4k+1}{81^{k+\frac12}},
\quad j_{6D}\left(\sqrt{\frac{-1}{2}}\right)=81</math>

==Level 7==

Define

:<math>s_{7A}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2\binom{2j}{k}\binom{k+j}{j} =1, 4, 48, 760, 13840,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A183204}})

and,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{7A}(\tau) &=\left(\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(7\tau)}\right)^{2}+7 \left(\frac{\eta(7\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right)^{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{q} +10 + 51q + 204q^2 +681q^3+\cdots\\
j_{7B}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(7\tau)}\right)^{4}= \frac{1}{q}- 4 + 2q + 8q^2 - 5q^3 - 4q^4 - 10q^5 + \cdots
\end{align}</math>

Example:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{22^3}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{7A}(k)\, \frac{11895k+1286}{\left(-22^3\right)^{k}},
\quad j_{7A}\left(\frac{7+\sqrt{-427}}{14}\right) = -22^3+1 = -\left(39\sqrt{7}\right)^2=-10647</math>

No pi formula has yet been found using '''''j'''''<sub>7B</sub>.

==Level 8==

===Modular functions===

Levels <math>2, 4, 8</math> are related since they are just powers of the same prime. Define,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{4B}(\tau)
&=\sqrt{j_{2A}(2\tau)} = \left( \sqrt{j_{4D}(\tau)} + \frac{8}{\sqrt{j_{4D}(\tau)}} \right)^2 -16 = \left( \sqrt{j_{8A}(\tau)} - \frac{4}{\sqrt{j_{8A}(\tau)}} \right)^2 = \left( \sqrt{j_{8A'}(\tau)} + \frac{4}{\sqrt{j_{8A'}(\tau)}} \right)^2\\
&=\left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(4\tau)}\right)^{12}+2^6 \left(\frac{\eta(4\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)}\right)^{12} = \frac{1}{q} + 52q + 834q^3 + 4760q^5 + 24703q^7+\cdots\\
j_{4D}(\tau)&= \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(4\tau)}\right)^{12} =\frac{1}{q} - 12q + 66q^3 - 232q^5 + 639q^7 - 1596q^9 + \cdots\\ 
j_{8A}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)\,\eta(4\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(8\tau)}\right)^{8}=\frac{1}{q} + 8 + 36q + 128q^2 + 386q^3 +1024q^4+\cdots\\
j_{8A'}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\,\eta^2(4\tau)}{\eta^2(2\tau)\,\eta(8\tau)}\right)^{8}=\frac{1}{q} - 8 + 36q - 128q^2 + 386q^3 -1024q^4+\cdots\\
j_{8B}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta^2(4\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\,\eta(8\tau)}\right)^{12}=\sqrt{j_{4A}(2\tau)}=\frac{1}{q} + 12q + 66q^3 + 232q^5 + 639q^7+\cdots\\
j_{8E}(\tau)&=\left(\frac{\eta^3(4\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\,\eta^2(8\tau)}\right)^{4} =\frac{1}{q} + 4q + 2q^3 - 8q^5 - q^7 + 20q^9 - 2q^{11} - 40q^{13} +\cdots
\end{align}</math>

Just like for level 6, five of these functions have a linear relationship,

:<math>j_{4B}-j_{4D}-j_{8A}-j_{8A'}+2j_{8E} = 0</math>

But this is not one of the nine Conway-Norton-Atkin linear dependencies since <math>j_{8A'}</math> is ''not'' a moonshine function. However, it is related to one as,

:<math>j_{8A'}(\tau) = -j_{8A}\Big(\tau+\tfrac12\Big)</math> 

===Sequences===

:<math>s_{4B}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k 4^{k-2j}\binom{k}{2j}\binom{2j}{j}^2 =\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}\binom{2k-2j}{k-j}\binom{2j}{j}=1, 8, 120, 2240, 47320,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{4D}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}^3=1, 8, 216, 8000, 343000,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{8A}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^2\binom{2j}{k}^2 =1, 4, 40, 544, 8536,\ldots</math>  ({{OEIS2C|id=A290575}})

:<math>s_{8B}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{2j}{j}^3\binom{2k-4j}{k-2j} =1, 2, 14, 36, 334,\ldots</math>

where the first is the product<ref name="Almkvist"/> of the central binomial coefficient and a sequence related to an [[arithmetic-geometric mean]] ({{OEIS2C|id=A081085}}).

===Identities===

The modular functions can be related as,

:<math> \pm\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{4B}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{4B}(\tau)+16\right)^{k+\frac12}} =  \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{4D}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{4D}(\tau)\right)^{2k+\frac12}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{8A}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{8A}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k s_{8A}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{8A'}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

if the series converges and signs chosen appropriately. Note also the different exponent of <math>\left(j_{4D}(\tau)\right)^{2k+\frac12}</math> from the others.

===Examples===

Recall that <math>j_{2A}\left(\tfrac\sqrt{-58}{2}\right)=396^4,</math> while <math>j_{4B}\left(\tfrac\sqrt{-58}{4}\right)=396^2</math>. Hence,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{13}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{4B}(k)\,\frac{70\cdot99\,k+579}{\left(396^2+16\right)^{k+\frac12}},\qquad j_{4B}\left(\frac\sqrt{-58}{4}\right)=396^2</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 2\sqrt{2}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{8A}(k)\,\frac{-222+70\sqrt{58}\,\left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(4\left(99+13\sqrt{58}\right)^{2}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\qquad j_{8A}\left(\frac\sqrt{-58}{4}\right)=4\left(99+13\sqrt{58}\right)^{2}=4U_{58}^2</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 2\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k s_{8A}(k)\,\frac{-222\sqrt{2}+13\times58\,\left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left(4\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)^{12}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\qquad j_{8A'}\left(\frac\sqrt{-58}{4}\right)=4\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)^{12}=4U_{2}^{12},</math>

For another level 8 example,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac1{16}\sqrt{\frac35}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{8B}(k)\,\frac{210k+43}{(64)^{k+\frac12}},\qquad j_{8B}\left(\frac\sqrt{-7}{4}\right)=2^6=64</math>

==Level 9==

Define,

:<math>\begin{align}
j_{3C}(\tau) &= \left(j(3\tau)\right)^\frac13 =-6+\left(\frac{\eta^2(3\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(9\tau)}\right)^6 -27 \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(9\tau)}{\eta^2(3\tau)}\right)^6=\frac{1}{q} + 248q^2 + 4124q^5 +34752q^8+\cdots\\
j_{9A}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta^2(3\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(9\tau)}\right)^6 = \frac{1}{q} + 6 + 27q + 86q^2 + 243q^3 + 594q^4+\cdots\\
\end{align}</math>

The expansion of the first is the McKay–Thompson series of class 3C (and related to the [[cube root]] of the [[j-invariant|j-function]]), while the second is that of class 9A. Let,

:<math>s_{3C}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k (-3)^{k-3j}\binom{k}{j}\binom{k-j}{j}\binom{k-2j}{j} =\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k(-3)^{k-3j}\binom{k}{3j}\binom{2j}{j}\binom{3j}{j} = 1, -6, 54, -420, 630,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{9A}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}^2\sum_{m=0}^j\binom{k}{m}\binom{j}{m}\binom{j+m}{k} =1, 3, 27, 309, 4059,\ldots</math>

where the first is the product of the central binomial coefficients and {{OEIS2C|id=A006077}} (though with different signs).

Examples:

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{-\boldsymbol{i}}{9}\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{3C}(k)\,\frac{602k+85}{\left(-960-12\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{3C}\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{-43}}{6}\right)=-960</math>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = 6\,\boldsymbol{i}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{9A}(k)\,\frac{4-\sqrt{129}\,\left(k+\frac12\right)}{\left( -3\sqrt{3U_{129}}\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{9A}\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{-43}}{6}\right)=-3\sqrt{3}\left(53\sqrt{3}+14\sqrt{43}\right) = -3\sqrt{3U_{129}}</math>

==Level 10==

===Modular functions===

Define,

:<math>\begin{align}j_{10A}(\tau) &=\left(\sqrt{j_{10D}(\tau)} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{j_{10D}(\tau)}}\right)^2 = \left(\sqrt{j_{6B}(\tau)} + \frac{4}{\sqrt{j_{10B}(\tau)}}\right)^2 = \left(\sqrt{j_{10C}(\tau)} + \frac{5}{\sqrt{j_{10C}(\tau)}}\right)^2-4  =\frac{1}{q} + 4 + 22q + 56q^2 +\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{10B}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\eta(10\tau)}\right)^{4}=\frac{1}{q} - 4 + 6q - 8q^2 + 17q^3 - 32q^4 +\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{10C}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(5\tau)\eta(10\tau)}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{q} - 2 - 3q + 6q^2 + 2q^3 + 2q^4+\cdots\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{10D}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\eta(10\tau)}\right)^{6}=\frac{1}{q} + 6 + 21q + 62q^2 + 162q^3 +\cdots
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}j_{10E}(\tau) &= \left(\frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta^5(5\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\eta^5(10\tau)}\right)=\frac{1}{q} + 1 + q + 2q^2 + 2q^3 - 2q^4 +\cdots\end{align}</math>

Just like <math>j_{6A}</math>, the function <math>j_{10A}</math> is a square or a near-square of the others. Furthermore, there are also linear relations between these,

:<math>T_{10A}-T_{10B}-T_{10C}-T_{10D}+2T_{10E} = 0</math>

or using the above eta quotients ''j''<sub>''n''</sub>,

:<math>j_{10A}-j_{10B}-j_{10C}-j_{10D}+2j_{10E} = 6</math>

===β sequences===

Let,

:<math>\beta_{1}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j}^4 =1, 2, 18, 164, 1810,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A005260}}, labeled as ''s''<sub>10</sub> in Cooper's paper)

:<math>\beta_{2}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{2j}{j}^{-1}\binom{k}{j}\sum_{m=0}^j \binom{j}{m}^4 =1, 4, 36, 424, 5716,\ldots</math>

:<math>\beta_{3}(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{2j}{j}^{-1}\binom{k}{j} (-4)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j \binom{j}{m}^4 =1, -6, 66, -876, 12786,\ldots</math>

their complements,

:<math>\beta_{2}'(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{2j}{j}^{-1}\binom{k}{j} (-1)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j \binom{j}{m}^4 =1, 0, 12, 24, 564, 2784,\ldots</math>

:<math>\beta_{3}'(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{2j}{j}^{-1}\binom{k}{j} (4)^{k-j}\sum_{m=0}^j \binom{j}{m}^4 =1, 10, 162, 3124, 66994,\ldots</math>

and,

:<math>s_{10B}(k)=1, -2, 10, -68, 514, -4100, 33940,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{10C}(k)=1, -1, 1, -1, 1, 23, -263, 1343, -2303,\ldots</math>

:<math>s_{10D}(k)=1, 3, 25, 267, 3249, 42795, 594145,\ldots</math>

though closed forms are not yet known for the last three sequences.

===Identities===

The modular functions can be related as,<ref>S. Cooper, "Level 10 analogues of Ramanujan’s series for 1/{{pi}}", Theorem 4.3, p.85, J. Ramanujan Math. Soc. 27, No.1 (2012)</ref>

:<math>U =
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_1(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10A}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}} = 
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_2(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10A}(\tau)+4\right)^{k+\frac12}} =
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_3(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10A}(\tau)-16\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

:<math>V =
\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{10B}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10B}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}} = 
\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{10C}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10C}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}} = 
\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{10D}(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10D}(\tau)\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

if the series converges. In fact, it can also be observed that,

:<math>U = V =\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_2'(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10A}(\tau)-4\right)^{k+\frac12}} =
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_3'(k)\,\frac{1}{\left(j_{10A}(\tau)+16\right)^{k+\frac12}}</math>

Since the exponent has a [[fractional part]], the sign of the [[square root]] must be chosen appropriately though it is less an issue when ''j''<sub>''n''</sub> is positive.

===Examples===

Just like level 6,  the level 10 function '''''j''<sub>10A</sub>''' can be used in three ways. Starting with,

:<math>j_{10A}\left(\sqrt{\frac{-19}{10}}\right) = 76^2 = 5776</math>

and noting that <math>5\cdot19=95</math> then,

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{5}{\sqrt{95}}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_1(k)\,\frac{408k+47}{\left(76^2\right)^{k+\frac12}}\\ 
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{1}{17\sqrt{95}}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_2(k)\,\frac{19\cdot 1824k+3983}{\left(76^2+4\right)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{1}{6\sqrt{95}}\,\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_3(k)\,\,\frac{19\cdot 646k+1427}{\left(76^2-16\right)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\end{align}</math>

as well as,

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{5}{481\sqrt{95}}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_2'(k)\,\frac{19\cdot 10336k+22675}{\left(76^2-4\right)^{k+\frac12}}\\
\frac{1}{\pi} &= \frac{5}{181\sqrt{95}}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty \beta_3'(k)\,\frac{19\cdot 3876k+8405}{\left(76^2+16\right)^{k+\frac12}}
\end{align}</math>

though the ones using the complements do not yet have a rigorous proof. A conjectured formula using one of the last three sequences is,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac{\boldsymbol{i}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{10C}(k)\frac{10k+3}{\left(-5^2\right)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{10C}\left(\frac{1+\,\boldsymbol{i}}{2}\right) = -5^2</math>

which implies there might be examples for all sequences of level 10.

==Level 11==

Define the McKay–Thompson series of class 11A,

:<math>j_{11A}(\tau)= (1+3F)^3+\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{F}}+3\sqrt{F}\right)^2=\frac{1}{q} + 6 + 17q + 46q^2 + 116q^3 +\cdots</math> 

or sequence ({{OEIS2C|id= A128525}}) and where,

:<math>F = \frac{\eta(3\tau)\,\eta(33\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\,\eta(11\tau)}</math>

and,

:<math>s_{11A}(k) = 1, 4, 28, 268, 3004, 36784, 476476,\ldots</math> ({{OEIS2C|id= A284756}})

No closed form in terms of binomial coefficients is yet known for the sequence but it obeys the [[recurrence relation]],

:<math>(k + 1)^3 s_{k + 1} = 2(2k + 1)\left(5k^2 + 5k + 2\right)s_k - 8k\left(7k^2 + 1\right)s_{k - 1} + 22k(k - 1)(2k - 1)s_{k - 2}</math>

with initial conditions ''s''(0) = 1, ''s''(1) = 4.

Example:<ref name = "Cooper 2">{{cite web |first=S. |last=Cooper |title=Ramanujan's theories of elliptic functions to alternative bases, and beyond |work=Askey 80 Conference |date=December 2013 |url=http://www-users.math.umn.edu/~stant001/ASKEYABS/Shaun_Cooper.pdf }}</ref>

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi}=\frac{\boldsymbol{i}}{22}\sum_{k=0}^\infty s_{11A}(k)\,\frac{221k+67}{(-44)^{k+\frac12}},\quad j_{11A}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt\frac{-17}{11}}{2}\right)=-44</math>

==Higher levels==

As pointed out by Cooper,<ref name = "Cooper 2" /> there are analogous sequences for certain higher levels.

==Similar series==

R. Steiner found examples using [[Catalan numbers]] <math>C_k </math>,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-n}\right)^2 \frac{(4z)k+\left(4^{2n-3}-(4n-3)z\right)}{16^k}\qquad z \in \Z,\quad n\ge2,\quad n \in \N </math>
and for this a [[modular form]] with a second periodic for ''k'' exists:
:<math>k=\frac{(-20-12\boldsymbol{i})+16n}{16},\qquad k=\frac{(-20+12\boldsymbol{i})+16n}{16}</math> 
Other similar series are 
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-2}\right)^2 \frac{3k+\frac14}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{(4z+1)k-z}{16^k} \qquad z \in \Z</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{-1k+\frac12}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{0k+\frac14}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{{\frac{k}{5}+\frac15}}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{{\frac{k}{3}+\frac16}}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{{\frac{k}{2}+\frac18}}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{2k-\frac14}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_{k-1}\right)^2 \frac{3k-\frac12}{16^k}</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(2C_k\right)^2 \frac{{\frac{k}{16}+\frac{1}{16}}}{16^k}</math>

with the last (comments in {{OEIS2C|id=A013709}}) found by using a [[linear combination]] of higher parts of [[Wallis product|Wallis]]-Lambert series for <math>\tfrac{4}{\pi}</math> and Euler series for the [[circumference of an ellipse]].

Using the definition of Catalan numbers with the [[gamma function]] the first and last for example give the identities

:<math>\frac14 = \sum_{k=0}^\infty {\left (\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac12+k\right)}{\Gamma(2+k)}\right)}^2 \left(4zk-(4n-3)z+4^{2n-3}\right)\qquad z \in \Z,\quad n\ge2,\quad n \in \N </math>
...
:<math>4 = \sum_{k=0}^\infty {\left (\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac12+k\right)}{\Gamma(2+k)}\right)}^2 (k+1)</math>.

The last is also equivalent to,

:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} = \frac14 \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\binom{2k}{k}^2}{k+1}\, \frac{1}{16^k}</math>

and is related to the fact that,

:<math> \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} \frac{16^k}{k \binom{2k}{k}^2} = \pi</math>

which is a consequence of [[Stirling's approximation]].
